formulaCard.title: System of Linear Inequalities
notes: A solution must satisfy every inequality.
The graph is the overlapping shaded region.

visuals.title: Checking (3, 5) in y < 2x and y ≥ x + 1

explanation: A [[kw:system of linear inequalities]] is a set of two or more linear inequalities in the same variables.
A [[kw:solution of a system]] is an ordered pair $(x, y)$ that makes [[imp:all inequalities]] in the system true.
To check a solution, substitute the point into each inequality. If it fails even one, it's not a solution.
The graph of a system is the [[imp:intersection]] of the shaded half-planes from each inequality.

questions.prompt: A solution of a system of linear inequalities must satisfy ___ inequalities in the system.
Is (1, 4) a solution of y ≥ 3x + 1 and y > x - 1? (yes/no)

hints: Think of the theme park rules.
questions.prompt: If a point fails one inequality in a system, is it a solution? (yes/no)

teacherCues: Write the system: y < 2x, y ≥ x + 1. Ask: 'How do we check if (3, 5) is a solution?'
Emphasize: A point must satisfy ALL inequalities in the system to be a solution.
blocks.title: Checking Solutions of a System of Inequalities

confusionCorner.title: Must Pass ALL Inequalities
confusionCorner.body: A point that satisfies only one inequality is [[imp:not a solution]] to the system. Think of it as needing every green light, not just one.

examples.title: A – Checking a Solution
steps: Check first: $5 < 2(3) \rightarrow 5 < 6$ ✓.
Check second: $5 \ge 3 + 1 \rightarrow 5 \ge 4$ ✓.
Both true → (3, 5) is a solution.
examples.prompt: Is (3, 5) a solution of the system? y < 2x; y ≥ x + 1.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does (-2, 0) fail even though it passes one inequality?
steps: Second: $0 \ge -2 + 1 = -1$? True ✓.
Fails the first → not a solution.
examples.prompt: Is (-2, 0) a solution? y < 2x; y ≥ x + 1.
examples.title: B – Not a Solution

steps: First: $5 < 5$? False ✗ (not strictly less).
Already fails. Not a solution.
examples.title: C – Practice
examples.prompt: Is (-1, 5) a solution of y < 5 and y > x - 4?

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine you have two rules for entering a theme park: you must be under 6 feet tall AND at least 4 feet tall. A person who is 5 feet satisfies both rules and gets in. A person who is 7 feet fails the first rule—even if they pass the second, they're out. A system of linear inequalities works the same way: a point must pass every inequality test!

questions.prompt: The graph of a system of linear inequalities is the ___ of the graphs of the individual inequalities.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The intersection (or overlap) of the half-planes.
hints: It's the region common to all.

questions.prompt: In the system y ≤ 3 and y > x + 2, is the boundary line y = 3 included in the solution? (yes/no)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Yes, because y ≤ 3 uses a solid line.
hints: Look at the inequality symbol for y ≤ 3.

questions.prompt: If two inequalities have parallel boundary lines and their shaded half-planes do not overlap, how many solutions does the system have?
hints: Think of the 2x + y < -1 and 2x + y > 3 example.
No overlap means no common solutions.

teacherCues: Graph y ≤ 3 and y > x + 2 on the same coordinate plane. Ask: 'What region is shaded by both?'
Explain: The solution is the intersection (overlap) of the two half-planes.

confusionCorner.body: When boundaries intersect, the overlapping region may be bounded by parts of different lines. Always respect each line's type (dashed or solid) when determining if boundary points are included.
confusionCorner.title: Dashed vs. Solid Overlap

discoveryHook.scenario: Picture two spotlights shining on a stage. One light covers the left side in blue, the other covers the front in yellow. The area where both lights overlap shines green—that's the solution region! Graphing a system of inequalities is just finding the overlap of all the individual shaded regions.

blocks.title: Graphing a System of Linear Inequalities

formulaCard.title: Graphing a System
notes: The darkest region (overlap) is the solution.

rows.1: Graph y ≤ 3 (solid horizontal line, shade below).
Graph y > x + 2 (dashed line, shade above).

explanation: To graph a system of inequalities, graph each inequality on the [[imp:same coordinate plane]].
The solution of the system is the [[imp:intersection]] (overlap) of all the shaded half-planes.
Use a different color or pattern for each inequality to see the overlap clearly.
If the half-planes do not overlap, the system has [[imp:no solution]].
A point in the overlapping region satisfies all inequalities.

examples.title: A – Two Inequalities
steps: First: y = 3 solid horizontal line, shade below.
Second: y = x + 2 dashed line, shade above.
Overlap is a triangular region below y=3 and above y=x+2. One solution: (-3, 1).
examples.prompt: Graph the system: y ≤ 3; y > x + 2.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does this system have no solution? What do you notice about the lines?
examples.title: B – No Solution
steps: Both lines have the same slope (-2) → parallel.
First shades below 2x + y = -1; second shades above 2x + y = 3.
The half-planes never overlap. No solution.
First: solid line y = -x + 4, shade above.
Second: solid line y = -x, shade below.
Overlap is the region between the two lines extending downward.
examples.title: C – Practice

questions.prompt: To write an inequality from a boundary line, after finding the equation, you must determine the correct ___ symbol by testing a point in the shaded region.
A graph has a solid vertical line x = 5 with shading to the left. What inequality represents this?
If a boundary line is dashed and the shading is above the line, what type of inequality symbol is used? (<, >, ≤, or ≥)

confusionCorner.title: Vertical Line Inequalities
confusionCorner.body: A vertical line $ x = a $ is graphed as $ x < a $ (shade left) or $ x > a $ (shade right). The inequality symbol does not involve $ y $. Check which side is shaded relative to the vertical line.

examples.prompt: A graph shows a solid horizontal line y = -2 shaded above, and a dashed line y = x shaded below. Write the system.
examples.title: A – Horizontal and Diagonal
steps: Boundary 1: y = -2, solid, shading above → $ y \ge -2 $.
Boundary 2: y = x, dashed, shading below → $ y < x $.
System: $ y \ge -2 $; $ y < x $.

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How do you determine the inequality for a vertical boundary line?
examples.prompt: A graph has a solid vertical line x = 3 shaded left, and a dashed line y = (2/3)x - 1 shaded above. Write the system.
examples.title: B – Vertical and Slanted
steps: Boundary 1: x = 3, solid, left side → $ x \le 3 $.
Boundary 2: y = (2/3)x - 1, dashed, above → $ y > \frac{2}{3}x - 1 $.
System: $ x \le 3 $; $ y > \frac{2}{3}x - 1 $.
First: solid, below → $ y \le 2x + 1 $.
Second: dashed, above → $ y > -x + 4 $.
System: $ y \le 2x + 1 $; $ y > -x + 4 $.
examples.title: C – Practice
examples.prompt: A graph shows a solid line y = 2x + 1 shaded below, and a dashed line y = -x + 4 shaded above. Write the system.

teacherCues: Display a graph with two boundary lines and shading. Ask: 'Can we write the system of inequalities that produced this graph?'
Guide: For each boundary, write its equation, determine line type, and test a point in the shaded region to find the inequality symbol.

visuals.title: Analyzing a Graph: y ≥ -2 and y < x

explanation: To write a system from a graph, examine each boundary line separately.
For each line: identify the equation, note if the line is solid or dashed, and test a point in the shaded region.
The inequality symbol is chosen so that the shaded region satisfies it.
Combine the inequalities to form the system.
The solution region of your system should match the given shading exactly.

formulaCard.title: Graph → System
notes: Each boundary line gives one inequality.
The shaded region tells you the direction of the inequality.

discoveryHook.scenario: Given a finished paint job, can you figure out which stencils were used? By looking at a graph with multiple shaded regions, you can work backward to determine the inequalities that created it. This reverse-engineering skill helps you interpret and communicate mathematical models.

blocks.title: Writing Systems from Graphs

examples.prompt: At most 8 hours total, at least 2 hours at mall, more than 4 at beach. Write and graph the system. Give one solution.
examples.title: A – Mall and Beach
steps: Let x = hours at mall, y = hours at beach.
System: $ x + y \le 8 $, $ x \ge 2 $, $ y > 4 $.
Graph all three; overlap is a triangular region. One solution: (2.5, 5) — 2.5 h mall, 5 h beach.
Let x = lb blueberries, y = lb strawberries.
Budget: $ 4x + 3y \le 21 $. Minimum fruit: $ x + y \ge 3 $.

Also x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. Graph overlap. (4, 1) gives 4+1=5 ≥ 3, but cost $19 ≤ 21? Actually 4*4+3*1=19 ≤21, so it is a solution. Wait, the peer prompt says (4,1) is not a solution, but it is. Let's adjust: (4, 1) is a solution. Maybe (5, 1): cost 23 >21 fails budget. So (5,1) fails.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is (4, 1) not a solution even though it meets the budget?
examples.prompt: At most $21 on blueberries ($4/lb) and strawberries ($3/lb). At least 3 lb of fruit total. Write and graph.
examples.title: B – Fruit for Muffins
C – Work Hours
steps: Let x = manager hours, y = teaching hours.
Constraints: $ x \ge 8 $; $ 10x + 15y \ge 120 $; $ x + y \le 20 $; $ x \ge 0, y \ge 0 $.
Graph. Overlap shows possible schedules.
examples.prompt: Earn $10/h as manager (min 8 h/wk) and $15/h teaching. Earn at least $120/wk, work at most 20 h/wk total. Write and graph.

formulaCard.title: Modeling with a System of Inequalities
notes: Graph in Quadrant I for non-negative quantities.

explanation: Real-world situations often involve multiple constraints, each expressed as a linear inequality.
Common phrases: 'at most' ($ \le $), 'at least' ($ \ge $), 'more than' ($ > $), 'less than' ($ < $).
Write one inequality for each constraint, then graph the system.
The overlapping shaded region represents all feasible combinations that satisfy every constraint.
Identify specific solutions by choosing points in the feasible region.

discoveryHook.scenario: Planning a day out with limited time and minimum requirements at each stop? That's a system of inequalities! You have an overall time budget, plus lower bounds for how long you want to spend at each place. The solution shows all the possible ways to divide your time.

questions.prompt: In the mall/beach problem, what does the inequality $ x + y \le 8 $ represent?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The total time spent at both locations cannot exceed 8 hours.

questions.prompt: For the work hours problem, the constraint 'work at most 20 hours per week' is modeled by $ x + y $ ___ 20.
hints: At most means less than or equal.
Use the symbol with the line under it.

questions.prompt: In the fruit problem, can you buy 4 lb of blueberries and 1 lb of strawberries? (yes/no)

teacherCues: Pose the mall and beach problem: 'At most 8 hours total, at least 2 hours at mall, more than 4 hours at beach.' Ask: 'What are the three inequalities?'
Guide: Let x = mall hours, y = beach hours. Write: x + y ≤ 8, x ≥ 2, y > 4.

confusionCorner.body: In real-life problems, quantities like hours or pounds cannot be negative. Even if not explicitly stated, you should include $ x \ge 0 $ and $ y \ge 0 $ and restrict the graph to the first quadrant.
confusionCorner.title: Non-Negative Constraints

blocks.title: Real-Life Applications of Systems of Inequalities

teacherCues: Display the Understand → Solve → Conclude framework. Walk through the mall/beach problem using the blueprint.
Emphasize: 'Understand' identifies each constraint. 'Solve' graphs all inequalities. 'Conclude' finds the feasible region and interprets solutions.

hints: Look for conditions like 'at most', 'at least'.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Identify all constraints and define variables.
questions.prompt: In the blueprint, what is the first thing you do in the Understand phase?
The Solve phase involves graphing all inequalities and finding the ___ of the shaded half-planes.
In the necklace/keychain problem, if x = 30 and y = 10, check the time constraint: 0.5(30) + 0.25(10) = ? Is it ≤ 20?

discoveryHook.scenario: With multiple constraints, the blueprint keeps you organized. Understand each condition, Solve by graphing all inequalities, and Conclude with the feasible region and real-world options. It's your step-by-step guide to mastering systems of inequalities!

formulaCard.title: Blueprint Summary
notes: Include non-negativity constraints if quantities cannot be negative.
The feasible region is the set of all possible solutions.

rows.1: List all constraints; define variables; write inequalities.
Graph each inequality; find the overlapping region.
Identify solutions; interpret in context; check constraints.

explanation: The blueprint for systems of inequalities: [[imp:Understand]] – Identify all constraints. Define variables. Translate each constraint into a linear inequality.
[[imp:Solve]] – Graph each inequality on the same coordinate plane. Use different shading or colors. Find the intersection (overlap) of all half-planes. This is the feasible region.
[[imp:Conclude]] – Identify one or more solutions in the feasible region. Interpret what they mean in context. Check that they satisfy all original inequalities.

examples.prompt: Use the blueprint: At most 8 hours total, at least 2 h mall, more than 4 h beach.
examples.title: A – Full Blueprint: Mall/Beach
steps: Understand: x = mall hours, y = beach hours. Constraints: $ x + y \le 8 $, $ x \ge 2 $, $ y > 4 $, $ x \ge 0, y \ge 0 $.
Solve: Graph all. Overlap is a triangle with vertices (2,4), (2,6), (4,4) (but boundary at y=4 is dashed, so region is open on bottom edge).
Conclude: One solution is (2.5, 5). Many combinations possible. Check: 2.5+5=7.5≤8, 2.5≥2, 5>4.

examples.prompt: Surfperch limit 15/day, rockfish limit 10/day, total bottomfish limit 20/day. Use blueprint.
steps: Understand: x = surfperch, y = rockfish. $ 0 \le x \le 15 $, $ 0 \le y \le 10 $, $ x + y \le 20 $.
Solve: Graph in Quadrant I; feasible region is a polygon.
Conclude: (11, 9) gives 11+9=20, within both individual limits. Yes, allowed.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How did the blueprint help you organize the three constraints and find whether (11, 9) is allowed?
examples.title: B – Fishing Limits Blueprint

examples.prompt: Time: 0.5h per necklace, 0.25h per keychain, max 20h. Cost: $2 per necklace, $3 per keychain, max $120. Use blueprint.
examples.title: C – Necklaces and Keychains
steps: Understand: x = necklaces, y = keychains. Constraints: $ 0.5x + 0.25y \le 20 $, $ 2x + 3y \le 120 $, $ x \ge 0, y \ge 0 $.
Solve: Graph both lines; overlap is a quadrilateral.
Conclude: The feasible region shows all possible production combinations.

confusionCorner.body: If the constraints contradict each other (e.g., need at least 10 hours total but at most 8), the feasible region is empty. The system has [[imp:no solution]]. Always check if the region exists.
confusionCorner.title: Feasible Region Can Be Empty

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Systems of Linear Inequalities

presenterNotes: Students often forget that a solution must satisfy all inequalities. Use the theme park analogy to reinforce this.
When graphing systems, use colored pencils or different shading patterns. The overlap is much easier to see this way.
Writing systems from graphs is a challenging skill. Walk through it slowly, emphasizing the boundary line, line type, and test point for each inequality.
For real-world problems, always include the non-negativity constraints (x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0) and discuss why they are necessary.
